questions.prompt: Which statements about C arrays and pointers are correct?
options: In most expressions, an array expression is converted to a pointer to its first element.
The sizeof operator applied directly to an array gives the size of its pointer.
Pointer arithmetic advances in units of the pointed-to type.
Two pointers into the same array can be subtracted to obtain an element distance.
answer: In most expressions, an array expression is converted to a pointer to its first element.
Pointer arithmetic advances in units of the pointed-to type.
Two pointers into the same array can be subtracted to obtain an element distance.
questions.explanation: Array-to-pointer conversion has exceptions such as sizeof. sizeof(array) measures the full array, while pointer arithmetic and subtraction are measured in elements.

questions.prompt: For the recursive definition T(n)=2T(n/2)+n, with T(1)=Θ(1) and n a power of 2, which statements are true?
options: The recursion tree has Θ(log n) levels.
The total non-recursive work at each level is Θ(n).
The total running time is Θ(n log n).
The recursion uses Θ(n) stack depth.
answer: The recursion tree has Θ(log n) levels.
The total non-recursive work at each level is Θ(n).
The total running time is Θ(n log n).
questions.explanation: Each split halves the problem, so there are Θ(log n) levels. The aggregate work per level is n, giving Θ(n log n); the recursion depth is logarithmic.

questions.prompt: For a two-dimensional array stored in row-major order, which statements are correct?

questions.prompt: Which standard comparison sort has Θ(n²) worst-case time but Θ(n log n) average-case time?
questions.explanation: Quicksort can partition extremely unevenly in the worst case, while balanced partitions give Θ(n log n) average time.

questions.prompt: How many comparisons does standard selection sort perform on 6 elements, independent of input order?
questions.explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted suffix at every pass; the total is 6(6−1)/2=15.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm is stable in its standard implementation?
questions.explanation: A stable merge procedure preserves the relative order of equal keys.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm can be implemented in-place with Θ(1) auxiliary array space and has Θ(n log n) worst-case time?
questions.explanation: Heapsort stores the heap in the input array and has a worst-case Θ(n log n) bound.

questions.prompt: Activities have finish times 1,2,…,4 and start times 0,1,…,3, respectively. Using the earliest-finish greedy rule, how many mutually compatible activities are selected?
questions.explanation: Each activity finishes exactly when the next starts, so all 4 activities can be selected.

questions.prompt: For the activity-selection problem, which greedy choice is optimal?
options: Choose the compatible activity with earliest finish time
Choose the activity with earliest start time
Choose the activity with maximum duration
answer: Choose the compatible activity with earliest finish time
questions.explanation: Choosing earliest finish leaves the largest remaining time interval; the choice can be justified by an exchange argument.

questions.prompt: A fractional knapsack has capacity 10. Items (weight,value) are (10,60), (20,100), (30,120). What value does the greedy value/weight rule obtain?
questions.explanation: Value densities are 6,5,4. Take the highest-density item first, then a fraction of the next item if needed.

questions.prompt: Which property is needed to justify a greedy algorithm for an optimization problem?
options: A greedy-choice property supporting an optimal solution
The input must be sorted already
Every subproblem must have equal size
The algorithm must use a priority queue
answer: A greedy-choice property supporting an optimal solution
questions.explanation: A greedy strategy needs a proof that a locally optimal choice can be part of a global optimum.

questions.prompt: A triangle has edge weights 6, 8, and 18. What is the weight of its minimum spanning tree?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree uses the two cheapest edges, 6 and 8; total=14.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is a greedy algorithm for finding a minimum spanning tree?
questions.explanation: Kruskal repeatedly selects the lightest edge that does not create a cycle.

questions.prompt: Why does Dijkstra’s greedy choice fail in the presence of arbitrary negative-weight edges?
options: A later path may reduce the distance to a vertex already finalized
It requires the graph to be complete
It always chooses the largest edge first
answer: A later path may reduce the distance to a vertex already finalized
questions.explanation: Negative edges can improve a finalized distance after the algorithm has committed to it.

questions.prompt: A Huffman tree is built from symbol frequencies 3,3,6,12. What is the first pair merged?
questions.explanation: Huffman’s algorithm first combines the two least frequent symbols.

questions.prompt: In Kruskal’s algorithm, which data structure efficiently detects whether an edge joins two components?
questions.explanation: Union–find supports component connectivity checks and merges efficiently.

questions.prompt: Which statements about greedy algorithms are correct?
options: A greedy-choice argument is needed to justify a locally optimal choice.
A greedy algorithm is correct for every problem with optimal substructure.
Kruskal’s algorithm adds a lightest safe edge.
Fractional knapsack is optimally solved by decreasing value-to-weight ratio.
answer: A greedy-choice argument is needed to justify a locally optimal choice.
Kruskal’s algorithm adds a lightest safe edge.
Fractional knapsack is optimally solved by decreasing value-to-weight ratio.
questions.explanation: Optimal substructure alone does not prove a greedy strategy correct. Kruskal and fractional knapsack have valid greedy-choice rules.
